Online Metric Matching with Unknown i.i.d. Arrivals

Tsubasa Harada
Institute of Science Tokyo
harada.t.30af@m.isct.ac.jp
November 3, 2026
Abstract

We study online metric matching with nn servers and nn requests drawn independently from an unknown distribution. Each request must be matched immediately and irrevocably to an unused server, and the algorithm receives no samples before the process starts. We give a randomized algorithm that is O⁡((log⁡log⁡log⁡n)2)O((\log\log\log n)^{2})-competitive on arbitrary metric spaces and O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive on tree metrics. These guarantees match the corresponding bounds for known i.i.d. request distributions in [5] up to constant factors. More generally, our competitive ratio is O⁡(α⁡(n))O(\alpha(n)) whenever the Fair-Bias algorithm introduced in that work has competitive ratio α⁡(n)\alpha(n) for known i.i.d. arrivals on the same class of metrics. Consequently, proving that Fair-Bias is constant-competitive on general metrics would also yield a constant-competitive algorithm for unknown i.i.d. arrivals.

1 Introduction

In online metric matching, nn servers are available in a metric space before the process begins, and nn requests arrive sequentially. Each request must be assigned to an unused server as soon as it arrives. Assignments cannot be changed later, and the objective is to minimize the total distance between requests and their assigned servers. The performance of an algorithm is measured by its competitive ratio, which compares its cost with the minimum cost of a perfect matching between all requests and all servers. Informally, an algorithm is α\alpha-competitive if its cost is at most α\alpha times the cost of a minimum-cost perfect matching.

Under adversarial arrivals, the optimal deterministic competitive ratio for general metrics is 2​n−12n-1 [6, 8], while randomized algorithms achieve O⁡(log2⁡n)O(\log^{2}n) [3].

When requests arrive at random, there are three natural models to consider. In the known-i.i.d. model, requests are drawn independently from a common distribution that is given to the algorithm before any requests arrive. In the unknown-i.i.d. model, requests are generated in the same way, but the distribution is not given to the algorithm. In the random-order model, an adversary fixes the request locations in advance without revealing them to the algorithm. The requests then arrive in a uniformly random order, and each location is revealed only upon arrival.

The known-i.i.d. model is no harder than the unknown-i.i.d. model, since an algorithm can ignore the supplied distribution. The unknown-i.i.d. model is in turn no harder than the random-order model: conditional on the multiset of i.i.d. requests, their order is uniformly random. Thus, any algorithm that is α\alpha-competitive in the random-order model is also α\alpha-competitive in the unknown-i.i.d. model.

For the known i.i.d. model, [5] obtain an O⁡((log⁡log⁡log⁡n)2)O((\log\log\log n)^{2}) competitive ratio for general metrics and O⁡(1)O(1) for tree metrics, whereas the optimal ratio in the random-order model is Θ⁡(log⁡n)\Theta(\log n) [11]. This gap raises a question also posed in [5, Section 5]: in terms of achievable competitive ratios, is the intermediate unknown-i.i.d. model closer to the known-i.i.d. model or the random-order model? For line metrics, [12] report an O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive algorithm in the unknown-i.i.d. model.11 1 Our account is based solely on the symposium abstract. We have not confirmed the full model assumptions or technical details. Their bound matches the known-i.i.d. bound on the line, providing a partial answer to this question.

1.1 Our result

In this paper, we give an algorithm for the unknown-i.i.d. model that matches the known-i.i.d. upper bound for general metrics. Let ALG\mathrm{ALG} denote the total matching cost incurred by the online algorithm, and let OPT\mathrm{OPT} denote the minimum cost of a perfect matching between all requests and servers.

Theorem 1.1.

For every metric space and every placement of nn labeled servers, there is a randomized online algorithm that, for every unknown request distribution DD, satisfies

𝔼⁡[ALG]≤O⁡((log⁡log⁡log⁡n)2)​𝔼​[OPT]\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{ALG}]\leq O((\log\log\log n)^{2})\,\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{OPT}]

when the nn requests are drawn i.i.d. from DD. Here, the expectation is over both the requests and the algorithm’s random choices.

More generally, our competitive ratio is O⁡(α⁡(n))O(\alpha(n)) whenever Fair-Bias has competitive ratio α⁡(n)\alpha(n) for known i.i.d. arrivals on the same class of metrics; see Theorem 6.2 and the reduction in Section 2.1. Thus, if the competitive ratio of Fair-Bias on general metrics is proved to be O⁡(1)O(1), our algorithm would also be O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive.

The resulting bound is o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n), so it separates unknown i.i.d. arrivals from random-order arrivals. It matches the order of the known-i.i.d. upper bound. On tree metrics, our algorithm is constant-competitive; see Corollary 6.3. The guarantees for the three arrival models are summarized in Table 1.

Note that our results do not imply that the optimal competitive ratios in the known-i.i.d. and unknown-i.i.d. models have the same asymptotic order. For example, a separation between the two models could still occur on general metrics if an algorithm other than Fair-Bias were O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive in the known-i.i.d. model while Fair-Bias had competitive ratio ω⁡(1)\omega(1).

1.2 Algorithm overview

Let δx\delta_{x} denote the point mass at xx and write

ν=1n​∑j=1nδsj\nu=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\delta_{s_{j}}

for the distribution obtained by choosing a server label uniformly, where sjs_{j} is the position of server jj. For a known request distribution DD, the reduction in [5, Lemma 2.1] uses an optimal transport plan from DD to ν\nu to generate virtual requests from ν\nu. This plan can be fixed before any requests arrive.

Our algorithm replaces DD in this construction by the empirical distribution

D^t=1t​∑i=1tδri,\widehat{D}_{t}=\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\delta_{r_{i}},

which includes the current request rtr_{t}. At each time tt, it computes an optimal transport plan from D^t\widehat{D}_{t} to ν\nu. Using the conditional probabilities in the row corresponding to the current request, it draws a virtual server label and passes it to Fair-Bias. The actual request rtr_{t} is assigned to the server chosen by Fair-Bias.

Although the transport plan changes as requests arrive, we prove that the generated virtual labels are independent and each is uniformly distributed over the nn server labels; see Lemma 5.1. Consequently, their positions form independent samples from ν\nu, so the guarantees of Fair-Bias apply to its execution on the virtual requests. It remains to bound the distances between actual and virtual requests. We show that their expected sum is at most O⁡(α⁡(n))​𝔼​[OPT]O(\alpha(n))\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{OPT}], where α⁡(n)\alpha(n) is the competitive ratio of Fair-Bias for independent requests from ν\nu; see Theorem 6.2.

1.3 Related work

Adversarial online metric matching.

[6] and [8] independently give deterministic (2​n−1)(2n-1)-competitive algorithms and matching lower bounds. For randomized algorithms, an Ω⁡(log⁡n)\Omega(\log n) lower bound is stated in [7]. [10] give an O⁡(log3⁡n)O(\log^{3}n)-competitive algorithm, and [3] improve this bound to O⁡(log2⁡n)O(\log^{2}n).

Random order and known i.i.d. arrivals.

[11] gives an O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n)-competitive algorithm and proves a matching Ω⁡(log⁡n)\Omega(\log n) lower bound in the random-order model. For known i.i.d. arrivals, [5] introduce Fair-Bias and obtain the O⁡((log⁡log⁡log⁡n)2)O((\log\log\log n)^{2}) general-metric bound, together with constant bounds on trees. [4] study uniform metric spaces and provide a more detailed competitive-ratio analysis under random-order arrivals.

In Euclidean spaces.

[2] study greedy matching on the line. They prove constant competitiveness when all server and request locations are sampled independently from the uniform distribution on [0,1][0,1]. When the server locations are chosen adversarially and the requests are still sampled independently from the uniform distribution on [0,1][0,1], they obtain an O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) competitive ratio. [13] obtain O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive algorithms for online metric matching in the known-i.i.d. model on [0,1]d[0,1]^{d}, under the uniform distribution in any fixed dimension and under distributions with densities bounded above by a constant in fixed dimensions d≥3d\geq 3. [9] analyze online metric matching with independent requests whose distributions need not be identical.

Separation between arrival models in other matching problems.

[1] separate random-order and unknown-i.i.d. arrivals for a different matching problem. They study non-bipartite minimum-cost matching on the line, where all participants arrive online. Upon each arrival, the algorithm either matches the new participant to a previously unmatched participant or leaves it unmatched for a future arrival. They obtain an O⁡(log2⁡n)O(\log^{2}n) competitive ratio under unknown i.i.d. arrivals, whereas the competitive ratio is unbounded under random-order arrivals.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 The model and benchmark

Let (X,d)(X,d) be an arbitrary metric space and let S=(s1,…,sn)S=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}) be the known server placement, with labels in [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}. Distinct server labels may occupy the same position. Each server can be used once. The requests r1,…,rnr_{1},\ldots,r_{n} are drawn independently from a distribution DD on XX, which is not given to the algorithm. The algorithm observes rtr_{t} before assigning it, can retain all previously observed requests, and receives no samples from DD before time 11.

For a request sequence R=(r1,…,rn)R=(r_{1},\ldots,r_{n}), define

OPT⁡(R,S)=min⁡∑t=1nσ∈𝔖n⁡d⁡(rt,sσ⁡(t)),\mathrm{OPT}(R,S)=\min_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\sum_{t=1}^{n}d(r_{t},s_{\sigma(t)}), (2.1)

where 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} is the set of permutations of [n][n]. We abbreviate this random variable by OPT\mathrm{OPT} when the placement and request distribution are understood. For an online algorithm, let ALG\mathrm{ALG} denote its total matching cost. An algorithm is c⁡(n)c(n)-competitive in the unknown-i.i.d. model if, for every SS and DD, its total cost satisfies 𝔼⁡[ALG]≤c⁡(n)​𝔼​[OPT]\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{ALG}]\leq c(n)\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{OPT}]. This is a ratio-of-expectations guarantee, not a bound on 𝔼⁡[ALG/OPT]\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{ALG}/\mathrm{OPT}] or on each realized request sequence.

Reduction to finite metric spaces.

We prove the result for finite metric spaces. For an arbitrary metric space, use the reduction in [10]: move each request to a nearest server location, run the algorithm on the resulting requests, and assign the original request to the same server as the transformed one. The nearest server is chosen among all nn servers, whether used or unused, with ties broken by a fixed order of labels. This converts a β\beta-competitive guarantee into a (2​β+1)(2\beta+1)-competitive guarantee, without changing its asymptotic order. Therefore, we assume that XX is finite in Sections 3, 4, 5 and 6.

2.2 Transport costs

Let δx\delta_{x} denote the point mass at xx. For probability distributions μ,η\mu,\eta on the finite metric space XX, let

μ=∑i∈Ipi​δxi,η=∑j∈Jqj​δyj,\mu=\sum_{i\in I}p_{i}\delta_{x_{i}},\qquad\eta=\sum_{j\in J}q_{j}\delta_{y_{j}},

where I,JI,J are finite index sets, (pi)i∈I(p_{i})_{i\in I} and (qj)j∈J(q_{j})_{j\in J} are probability vectors, and xi,yj∈Xx_{i},y_{j}\in X. The positions in either representation need not be distinct. Define

W1​(μ,η)=minγ≥0\displaystyle W_{1}(\mu,\eta)=\min_{\gamma\geq 0} ∑i∈I∑j∈Jγ⁡(i,j)​d​(xi,yj)\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}\gamma(i,j)d(x_{i},y_{j}) (2.2)
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} ∑j∈Jγ⁡(i,j)=pi\displaystyle\sum_{j\in J}\gamma(i,j)=p_{i} (i∈I),\displaystyle(i\in I),
∑i∈Iγ⁡(i,j)=qj\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}\gamma(i,j)=q_{j} (j∈J).\displaystyle(j\in J).

The variable γ⁡(i,j)\gamma(i,j) is the mass sent from source index ii at xix_{i} to destination index jj at yjy_{j}. A feasible matrix γ=(γ⁡(i,j))i∈I,j∈J\gamma=(\gamma(i,j))_{i\in I,j\in J} is called a transport plan. Its row indexed by ii sums to pip_{i}, and its column indexed by jj sums to qjq_{j}. When I=JI=J and xi=yix_{i}=y_{i} for every ii, a diagonal entry γ⁡(i,i)\gamma(i,i) represents mass left at the same position.

Let ν\nu be the uniform distribution over the nn server labels, and let D^t\widehat{D}_{t} be the empirical distribution of the first tt requests:

ν=1n​∑j=1nδsj,D^t=1t​∑i=1tδri.\nu=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\delta_{s_{j}},\qquad\widehat{D}_{t}=\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\delta_{r_{i}}. (2.3)

We will use the fact that common mass can be left at the same index in an optimal plan; see Lemma A.1.

The following lemma expresses the optimal matching cost as a transport cost.

Lemma 2.1.

For every realized request sequence RR,

n​W1​(D^n,ν)=OPT⁡(R,S).nW_{1}(\widehat{D}_{n},\nu)=\mathrm{OPT}(R,S).
Proof.

Sending mass 1/n1/n along each edge of a perfect matching gives a feasible transport plan, so n​W1​(D^n,ν)≤OPT⁡(R,S)nW_{1}(\widehat{D}_{n},\nu)\leq\mathrm{OPT}(R,S). For the reverse inequality, let π\pi be an optimal plan in (2.2) from D^n\widehat{D}_{n} to ν\nu, with rows indexed by requests i∈[n]i\in[n] and columns by servers j∈[n]j\in[n]. Every row and column sums to 1/n1/n, so n​πn\pi is doubly stochastic. A convex decomposition of n​πn\pi into permutation matrices therefore contains a permutation of cost at most n​W1​(D^n,ν)nW_{1}(\widehat{D}_{n},\nu). This permutation gives a perfect matching, proving the reverse inequality. ∎

For the analysis, we introduce two expected transport costs. Let I1,…,InI_{1},\ldots,I_{n} be drawn independently from the uniform distribution on [n][n] and put zt=sItz_{t}=s_{I_{t}}. This sequence of requests from ν\nu is separate from the unknown request sequence. Define

ν^t=1t∑i=1tδzi,ft=𝔼[W1(ν^t,ν)](1≤t≤n).\widehat{\nu}_{t}=\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\delta_{z_{i}},\qquad f_{t}=\mathbb{E}[W_{1}(\widehat{\nu}_{t},\nu)]\quad(1\leq t\leq n). (2.4)

For nonempty A⊆[n]A\subseteq[n], write

νA=1|A|​∑i∈Aδsi.\nu_{A}=\frac{1}{|A|}\sum_{i\in A}\delta_{s_{i}}.

Let 𝒰k\mathcal{U}_{k} be the uniform distribution over all kk-element subsets of [n][n], and define

gk=𝔼A∼𝒰k​[W1​(νA,ν)](1≤k≤n).g_{k}=\mathbb{E}_{A\sim\mathcal{U}_{k}}[W_{1}(\nu_{A},\nu)]\quad(1\leq k\leq n). (2.5)

In particular, gn=0g_{n}=0, although fnf_{n} need not be zero. Both definitions continue to distinguish co-located labels. If OPTν\mathrm{OPT}_{\nu} denotes the offline cost for nn i.i.d. requests from ν\nu, Lemma 2.1 gives

𝔼⁡[OPTν]=n​fn.\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{OPT}_{\nu}]=nf_{n}. (2.6)

3 The Fair-Bias algorithm

We recall Fair-Bias [5, Algorithm 1] for requests drawn independently from ν\nu. All numbered statements cited from [5] refer to its full version, arXiv:1904.09284v1.

3.1 Definition of Fair-Bias

Suppose F⊆[n]F\subseteq[n] is the current set of unused servers and k=|F|k=|F|. Fix an optimal plan ρF\rho_{F} from ν\nu to νF\nu_{F} by solving

minρF≥0\displaystyle\min_{\rho_{F}\geq 0} ∑j=1n∑i∈FρF​(j,i)​d​(sj,si)\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{i\in F}\rho_{F}(j,i)d(s_{j},s_{i}) (3.1)
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} ∑i∈FρF​(j,i)=1n\displaystyle\sum_{i\in F}\rho_{F}(j,i)=\frac{1}{n} (j∈[n]),\displaystyle(j\in[n]),
∑j=1nρF​(j,i)=1k\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{n}\rho_{F}(j,i)=\frac{1}{k} (i∈F).\displaystyle(i\in F).

Rows index input server labels j∈[n]j\in[n], and columns index available server labels i∈Fi\in F. The rule selecting an optimal plan depends only on FF and SS, not on the current input label. On input label jj, Fair-Bias chooses server i∈Fi\in F with probability n​ρF​(j,i)n\rho_{F}(j,i) and removes ii from FF. The optimal value in (3.1) is W1​(ν,νF)=W1​(νF,ν)W_{1}(\nu,\nu_{F})=W_{1}(\nu_{F},\nu), denoted by M⁡(F)M(F) in [5].

3.2 Properties and competitive-ratio bounds

Run Fair-Bias on the labels I1,…,InI_{1},\ldots,I_{n} drawn independently from the uniform distribution on [n][n]. Let AtA_{t} be the set of server labels it uses for the first tt requests, and let LtL_{t} be the total cost of those tt assignments.

Lemma 3.1 (A version of [5, Lemma 2.2]).

For every t∈[n]t\in[n],

At∼𝒰t,𝔼⁡[Lt]=∑k=n−t+1ngk.A_{t}\sim\mathcal{U}_{t},\qquad\mathbb{E}[L_{t}]=\sum_{k=n-t+1}^{n}g_{k}. (3.2)

In particular, 𝔼⁡[Ln]=∑k=1ngk\mathbb{E}[L_{n}]=\sum_{k=1}^{n}g_{k}.

Proof.

Condition on the past input labels and past internal random choices. The free set FF is then fixed, and the next input label remains uniformly distributed on [n][n] and independent of that past. For each i∈Fi\in F, its probability of being chosen next is

∑j=1n1n​n​ρF​(j,i)=1|F|.\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1}{n}\,n\rho_{F}(j,i)=\frac{1}{|F|}.

Hence the successive server labels are a uniformly random permutation of [n][n], and At∼𝒰tA_{t}\sim\mathcal{U}_{t}. Under the same conditioning, the expected next assignment cost is

∑j=1n1n​∑i∈Fn​ρF​(j,i)​d​(sj,si)=W1​(νF,ν).\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in F}n\rho_{F}(j,i)d(s_{j},s_{i})=W_{1}(\nu_{F},\nu).

When |F|=k|F|=k, the unconditional distribution of FF is 𝒰k\mathcal{U}_{k}, so the unconditional expected cost of that step is gkg_{k}. The first tt steps use free sets of sizes n,n−1,…,n−t+1n,n-1,\ldots,n-t+1, giving the stated sum. ∎

The assertion At∼𝒰tA_{t}\sim\mathcal{U}_{t} is a statement about the distribution without conditioning on the requests. It does not state that AtA_{t} is independent of ν^t\widehat{\nu}_{t}. In general these variables are dependent.

We also use the following competitive-ratio bounds.

Proposition 3.2 ([5, Theorems 3.10 and 4.6]).

For every server placement, Fair-Bias with requests drawn independently from ν\nu satisfies

∑k=1ngk=𝔼⁡[Ln]≤α⁡(n)​𝔼​[OPTν],α⁡(n)=O⁡((log⁡log⁡log⁡n)2).\sum_{k=1}^{n}g_{k}=\mathbb{E}[L_{n}]\leq\alpha(n)\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{OPT}_{\nu}],\qquad\alpha(n)=O((\log\log\log n)^{2}). (3.3)

For tree metrics, one may take α⁡(n)=4\alpha(n)=4.

4 Comparing cumulative transport costs

We prove (4.6) using the execution of Fair-Bias on independent requests from ν\nu in Section 3. Only Lemma 3.1 is used in this section; the competitive-ratio bound (3.3) is not needed until the comparison has been established.

We first relate gkg_{k} to gn−kg_{n-k}. The following identity is also used in the proof of [5, Lemma 3.9, Appendix C.3].

Lemma 4.1.

If 1≤k<n1\leq k<n and A⊆[n]A\subseteq[n] has size kk, then, writing Ac=[n]∖AA^{c}=[n]\setminus A,

k​W1​(νA,ν)=(n−k)​W1​(νAc,ν).kW_{1}(\nu_{A},\nu)=(n-k)W_{1}(\nu_{A^{c}},\nu). (4.1)

Consequently,

k​gk=(n−k)​gn−k.kg_{k}=(n-k)g_{n-k}. (4.2)
Proof.

Use server labels on both sides of the transport plans. By Lemma A.1, an optimal plan from νA\nu_{A} to ν\nu may leave mass 1/n1/n at each label of AA. After removing these zero-cost diagonal entries, the remaining plan has entries γi​j\gamma_{ij} only for i∈Ai\in A, j∈Acj\in A^{c}, with

∑j∈Acγi​j=1k−1n=n−kk​n(i∈A),∑i∈Aγi​j=1n(j∈Ac).\sum_{j\in A^{c}}\gamma_{ij}=\frac{1}{k}-\frac{1}{n}=\frac{n-k}{kn}\quad(i\in A),\qquad\sum_{i\in A}\gamma_{ij}=\frac{1}{n}\quad(j\in A^{c}). (4.3)

Conversely, any nonnegative matrix (γi​j)i∈A,j∈Ac(\gamma_{ij})_{i\in A,j\in A^{c}} satisfying (4.3) can be completed to a feasible plan by restoring those diagonal entries. Thus W1​(νA,ν)W_{1}(\nu_{A},\nu) is exactly the minimum cost over such matrices.

For transport from νAc\nu_{A^{c}} to ν\nu, leave mass 1/n1/n at each label of AcA^{c}. After removing these diagonal entries, the remaining entries ηj​i\eta_{ji} must satisfy

∑i∈Aηj​i=1n−k−1n=kn⁡(n−k)(j∈Ac),∑j∈Acηj​i=1n(i∈A).\sum_{i\in A}\eta_{ji}=\frac{1}{n-k}-\frac{1}{n}=\frac{k}{n(n-k)}\quad(j\in A^{c}),\qquad\sum_{j\in A^{c}}\eta_{ji}=\frac{1}{n}\quad(i\in A). (4.4)

Given a feasible γ\gamma in (4.3), set

ηj​i=kn−k​γi​j.\eta_{ji}=\frac{k}{n-k}\gamma_{ij}.

Its row and column sums are, respectively,

∑i∈Aηj​i=kn−k⋅1n=kn⁡(n−k),∑j∈Acηj​i=kn−k⋅n−kk​n=1n.\sum_{i\in A}\eta_{ji}=\frac{k}{n-k}\cdot\frac{1}{n}=\frac{k}{n(n-k)},\qquad\sum_{j\in A^{c}}\eta_{ji}=\frac{k}{n-k}\cdot\frac{n-k}{kn}=\frac{1}{n}.

It is therefore feasible for (4.4). By symmetry of the distance, its cost is

∑j∈Ac∑i∈Aηj​i​d​(sj,si)=kn−k​∑i∈A∑j∈Acγi​j​d​(si,sj).\sum_{j\in A^{c}}\sum_{i\in A}\eta_{ji}d(s_{j},s_{i})=\frac{k}{n-k}\sum_{i\in A}\sum_{j\in A^{c}}\gamma_{ij}d(s_{i},s_{j}).

The inverse transformation is γi​j=((n−k)/k)​ηj​i\gamma_{ij}=((n-k)/k)\eta_{ji}. Its feasibility follows by checking the row and column sums in the same way. Hence the two optimal residual costs differ by exactly the factor k/(n−k)k/(n-k), proving (4.1). Finally, complementation maps a uniform kk-element subset to a uniform (n−k)(n-k)-element subset. Taking expectations gives (4.2). ∎

We next bound ftf_{t} using the first tt assignments made by Fair-Bias.

Lemma 4.2.

For every t∈[n]t\in[n],

ft≤gt+1t​∑k=n−t+1ngk.f_{t}\leq g_{t}+\frac{1}{t}\sum_{k=n-t+1}^{n}g_{k}. (4.5)
Proof.

Consider the execution of Fair-Bias on independent requests from ν\nu defining AtA_{t} and LtL_{t} in Lemma 3.1. For each realization, send mass 1/t1/t along each of its first tt assignment edges. The source distribution is ν^t\widehat{\nu}_{t}; the destination distribution is νAt\nu_{A_{t}}, because these tt servers are distinct. Thus

W1​(ν^t,νAt)≤Ltt,W_{1}(\widehat{\nu}_{t},\nu_{A_{t}})\leq\frac{L_{t}}{t},

and the triangle inequality gives

W1​(ν^t,ν)≤Ltt+W1​(νAt,ν).W_{1}(\widehat{\nu}_{t},\nu)\leq\frac{L_{t}}{t}+W_{1}(\nu_{A_{t}},\nu).

Take expectation over this same execution, including the requests drawn from ν\nu and the internal random choices. The left-hand expectation is ftf_{t}, since that term depends only on the requests. The last term depends only on AtA_{t}, so its expectation is gtg_{t} by the unconditional distribution At∼𝒰tA_{t}\sim\mathcal{U}_{t}. Using Lemma 3.1 for the middle term yields

ft≤1t​𝔼​[Lt]+gt=1t​∑k=n−t+1ngk+gt.f_{t}\leq\frac{1}{t}\mathbb{E}[L_{t}]+g_{t}=\frac{1}{t}\sum_{k=n-t+1}^{n}g_{k}+g_{t}.

Neither taking expectations nor evaluating these individual terms requires independence between AtA_{t} and ν^t\widehat{\nu}_{t}. ∎

Summing the preceding bounds over time and using Lemma 4.1 gives the following theorem.

Theorem 4.3.

For every server placement,

∑t=1nft≤2​∑k=1ngk.\sum_{t=1}^{n}f_{t}\leq 2\sum_{k=1}^{n}g_{k}. (4.6)
Proof.

The claim is immediate for n=1n=1, since f1=g1=0f_{1}=g_{1}=0. For n≥2n\geq 2, sum (4.5) over tt:

∑t=1nft≤∑t=1ngt+∑t=1n1t​∑k=n−t+1ngk.\sum_{t=1}^{n}f_{t}\leq\sum_{t=1}^{n}g_{t}+\sum_{t=1}^{n}\frac{1}{t}\sum_{k=n-t+1}^{n}g_{k}. (4.7)

Since gn=0g_{n}=0, reversing the order of summation gives

∑t=1n1t​∑k=n−t+1ngk=∑k=1n−1gk​∑t=n−k+1n1t.\sum_{t=1}^{n}\frac{1}{t}\sum_{k=n-t+1}^{n}g_{k}=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}g_{k}\sum_{t=n-k+1}^{n}\frac{1}{t}.

The inner sum has kk terms, each at most 1/(n−k+1)1/(n-k+1). By (4.2),

∑k=1n−1gk​∑t=n−k+1n1t\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}g_{k}\sum_{t=n-k+1}^{n}\frac{1}{t} ≤∑k=1n−1kn−k+1​gk\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\frac{k}{n-k+1}g_{k}
=∑k=1n−1n−kn−k+1​gn−k\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\frac{n-k}{n-k+1}g_{n-k}
=∑j=1n−1jj+1​gj≤∑j=1ngj.\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\frac{j}{j+1}g_{j}\leq\sum_{j=1}^{n}g_{j}.

Substituting into (4.7) proves the theorem. ∎

Combining the theorem with (3.3) and (2.6) gives

∑t=1nft≤2​α​(n)​𝔼​[OPTν]=2​α​(n)​n​fn.\sum_{t=1}^{n}f_{t}\leq 2\alpha(n)\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{OPT}_{\nu}]=2\alpha(n)nf_{n}. (4.8)

5 Generating virtual requests

We return to the actual requests r1,…,rnr_{1},\ldots,r_{n} from the unknown distribution DD. The algorithm uses two different transport plans: an optimal transport plan πt\pi_{t} from D^t\widehat{D}_{t} to ν\nu that generates a virtual request rt′r^{\prime}_{t} from the actual request rtr_{t}, and the plan ρF\rho_{F} used by Fair-Bias to match that virtual request to an available server.

5.1 The algorithm and plan-selection rules

At time tt, choose an optimal plan πt\pi_{t} from D^t\widehat{D}_{t} to ν\nu in (2.2), with rows indexed by requests i∈[t]i\in[t] at rir_{i} and columns by server labels j∈[n]j\in[n] at sjs_{j}. Thus

∑j=1nπt​(i,j)=1t(i∈[t]),∑i=1tπt​(i,j)=1n(j∈[n]).\sum_{j=1}^{n}\pi_{t}(i,j)=\frac{1}{t}\quad(i\in[t]),\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{t}\pi_{t}(i,j)=\frac{1}{n}\quad(j\in[n]).

We use any fixed tie-breaking rule that selects the same transport plan whenever the request locations coincide as multisets.

Having observed rtr_{t}, draw a virtual label Jt∈[n]J_{t}\in[n] with probabilities

ℙ⁡(Jt=j∣r1,…,rt)=t​πt​(t,j),j∈[n],\mathbb{P}(J_{t}=j\mid r_{1},\ldots,r_{t})=t\pi_{t}(t,j),\qquad j\in[n], (5.1)

and set rt′=sJtr^{\prime}_{t}=s_{J_{t}}. These probabilities are nonnegative and sum to one because row tt of πt\pi_{t} sums to 1/t1/t. The draw uses fresh randomness independent of the request sequence and the randomness used to draw the virtual labels at other times.

Pass JtJ_{t} to Fair-Bias, whose plan ρF\rho_{F} is allowed to depend on the current free set FF. Use randomness for Fair-Bias that is independent of the request sequence and of all randomness used to draw the virtual labels. If Fair-Bias selects label ata_{t}, assign the actual request rtr_{t} to that same server. Fair-Bias bases its decisions only on its virtual inputs, its own state, and its own randomness; it does not inspect the original request history.

The virtual label JtJ_{t} does not specify the final assignment and may refer to a server that has already been used. The transport plans can be computed using only the observed request positions and the known server locations.

5.2 Independence of the virtual sequence

We first show that the virtual requests r1′,…,rn′r^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,r^{\prime}_{n} are independent samples from ν\nu. For a fixed multiset of requests M={x1,…,xt}M=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{t}\}, write πM​(i,j)\pi_{M}(i,j) for the selected plan, with row ii corresponding to request xix_{i}.

Lemma 5.1.

Fix t≤nt\leq n and any multiset MM of tt requests. Present these requests in a uniformly random order and apply the conversion rule above. For every j1,…,jt∈[n]j_{1},\ldots,j_{t}\in[n],

ℙ⁡(J1=j1,…,Jt=jt)=n−t.\mathbb{P}(J_{1}=j_{1},\ldots,J_{t}=j_{t})=n^{-t}. (5.2)

Consequently, for i.i.d. actual requests, J1,…,JnJ_{1},\ldots,J_{n} are independent and each is uniformly distributed on [n][n], and r1′,…,rn′r^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,r^{\prime}_{n} are independent samples from ν\nu.

Proof.

We prove the lemma by induction on tt, simultaneously over all multisets of size tt. For t=1t=1, the plan has πM​(1,j)=1/n\pi_{M}(1,j)=1/n for every server label jj, so the base case follows.

For the inductive step, fix M={x1,…,xt}M=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{t}\}. Let KK be the index of the final request, so ℙ⁡(K=i)=1/t\mathbb{P}(K=i)=1/t for every i∈[t]i\in[t]. Conditional on K=iK=i, the preceding requests are a uniformly random ordering of the remaining t−1t-1 requests. By the induction hypothesis,

ℙ⁡(J1=j1,…,Jt−1=jt−1∣K=i)=n−(t−1).\mathbb{P}(J_{1}=j_{1},\ldots,J_{t-1}=j_{t-1}\mid K=i)=n^{-(t-1)}. (5.3)

By the conversion rule, we have

ℙ⁡(Jt=jt∣K=i,J1=j1,…,Jt−1=jt−1)=t​πM​(i,jt).\mathbb{P}(J_{t}=j_{t}\mid K=i,J_{1}=j_{1},\ldots,J_{t-1}=j_{t-1})=t\pi_{M}(i,j_{t}). (5.4)

Therefore,

ℙ⁡(J1=j1,…,Jt=jt)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(J_{1}=j_{1},\ldots,J_{t}=j_{t}) =∑i=1t1t​n−(t−1)​t​πM​(i,jt)=n−(t−1)​∑i=1tπM​(i,jt)=n−t.\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{t}\frac{1}{t}\,n^{-(t-1)}\,t\pi_{M}(i,j_{t})=n^{-(t-1)}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\pi_{M}(i,j_{t})=n^{-t}.

The last equality is the destination constraint for server label jtj_{t}. This completes the induction. ∎

By Lemma 5.1, the virtual requests r1′,…,rn′r^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,r^{\prime}_{n} generated in Section 5.1 are i.i.d. samples from ν\nu. They are also independent of the internal randomness of Fair-Bias, so the analysis in Section 3 applies to the execution of Fair-Bias on the virtual requests.

5.3 The conversion cost

We next relate the expected cost of converting an actual request to a virtual request to the expected transport cost between D^t\widehat{D}_{t} and ν\nu.

Lemma 5.2.

For each t∈[n]t\in[n],

𝔼⁡[d⁡(rt,rt′)]=𝔼⁡[W1​(D^t,ν)].\mathbb{E}[d(r_{t},r^{\prime}_{t})]=\mathbb{E}[W_{1}(\widehat{D}_{t},\nu)]. (5.5)
Proof.

Let Mt={r1,…,rt}M_{t}=\{r_{1},\ldots,r_{t}\} be the multiset of the first tt actual requests. Conditioned on Mt=M={x1,…,xt}M_{t}=M=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{t}\}, each request has probability 1/t1/t of being the final request. When request xix_{i} is last, its virtual label is drawn with probabilities t​πM​(i,j)t\pi_{M}(i,j). Thus

𝔼⁡[d⁡(rt,rt′)∣Mt=M]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[d(r_{t},r^{\prime}_{t})\mid M_{t}=M] =1t​∑i=1t∑j=1nt​πM​(i,j)​d​(xi,sj)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\sum_{j=1}^{n}t\pi_{M}(i,j)d(x_{i},s_{j})
=∑i=1t∑j=1nπM​(i,j)​d​(xi,sj)=W1​(D^t,ν).\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{t}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\pi_{M}(i,j)d(x_{i},s_{j})=W_{1}(\widehat{D}_{t},\nu).

The last equality uses optimality of πM\pi_{M}. Averaging over MtM_{t} yields the lemma. ∎

Let ALGν=∑t=1nd⁡(rt′,sat)\mathrm{ALG}_{\nu}=\sum_{t=1}^{n}d(r^{\prime}_{t},s_{a_{t}}) be the cost of running Fair-Bias on the virtual requests. For each realization, the triangle inequality yields d⁡(rt,sat)≤d⁡(rt,rt′)+d⁡(rt′,sat)d(r_{t},s_{a_{t}})\leq d(r_{t},r^{\prime}_{t})+d(r^{\prime}_{t},s_{a_{t}}). Summing and using Lemmas 5.2, 5.1 and 3.1, we obtain

𝔼⁡[ALG]≤∑t=1n𝔼⁡[W1​(D^t,ν)]+𝔼⁡[ALGν]=∑t=1n𝔼⁡[W1​(D^t,ν)]+∑k=1ngk.\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{ALG}]\leq\sum_{t=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}[W_{1}(\widehat{D}_{t},\nu)]+\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{ALG}_{\nu}]=\sum_{t=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}[W_{1}(\widehat{D}_{t},\nu)]+\sum_{k=1}^{n}g_{k}. (5.6)

6 Competitive analysis

We now compare the two terms in (5.6) with the expected offline optimum for the actual requests. The unknown distribution DD is used only in the analysis.

Lemma 6.1.

For every server placement and request distribution DD,

n​W1​(D,ν)\displaystyle nW_{1}(D,\nu) ≤𝔼⁡[OPT],\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{OPT}], (6.1)
𝔼⁡[W1​(D^t,ν)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[W_{1}(\widehat{D}_{t},\nu)] ≤W1​(D,ν)+ft\displaystyle\leq W_{1}(D,\nu)+f_{t} (1≤t≤n),\displaystyle(1\leq t\leq n), (6.2)
𝔼⁡[OPTν]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{OPT}_{\nu}] ≤𝔼⁡[OPT]+n​W1​(D,ν)≤2​𝔼​[OPT].\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{OPT}]+nW_{1}(D,\nu)\leq 2\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{OPT}]. (6.3)
Proof.

Write X={x1,…,xm}X=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}\} and D=∑a=1mpa​δxaD=\sum_{a=1}^{m}p_{a}\delta_{x_{a}}. For (6.1), fix an optimal matching σR\sigma_{R} for each realization RR and define a plan on [m]×[n][m]\times[n] by

βR​(a,j)=1n​∑i=1n𝟏​{ri=xa,σR​(i)=j}.\beta_{R}(a,j)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{r_{i}=x_{a},\ \sigma_{R}(i)=j\}.

The expected plan 𝔼⁡[βR]\mathbb{E}[\beta_{R}] has row sums pap_{a} and column sums 1/n1/n, so it is a feasible plan from DD to ν\nu. Since its cost is 𝔼⁡[OPT]/n\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{OPT}]/n, (6.1) is proved.

Next fix an optimal plan γ\gamma from DD to ν\nu in (2.2), with source indices a∈[m]a\in[m] at xax_{a} and destination indices j∈[n]j\in[n] at sjs_{j}. Independently for each i∈[n]i\in[n], draw an index pair (Ui,Vi)∈[m]×[n](U_{i},V_{i})\in[m]\times[n] with probabilities

ℙ⁡(Ui=a,Vi=j)=γ⁡(a,j)(a∈[m],j∈[n]),\mathbb{P}(U_{i}=a,V_{i}=j)=\gamma(a,j)\quad(a\in[m],\ j\in[n]),

and set r~i=xUi\widetilde{r}_{i}=x_{U_{i}} and zi=sViz_{i}=s_{V_{i}}. The sequence (r~i)i∈[n](\widetilde{r}_{i})_{i\in[n]} is i.i.d. from DD, and (zi)i∈[n](z_{i})_{i\in[n]} is i.i.d. from ν\nu. For each tt, the empirical distribution of r~1,…,r~t\widetilde{r}_{1},\ldots,\widetilde{r}_{t} follows D^t\widehat{D}_{t}. In addition, the empirical distribution of z1,…,ztz_{1},\ldots,z_{t} follows ν^t\widehat{\nu}_{t} and we have 𝔼⁡[d⁡(r~i,zi)]=W1​(D,ν)\mathbb{E}[d(\widetilde{r}_{i},z_{i})]=W_{1}(D,\nu). For each realization and each tt, define a plan λt\lambda_{t} with source r~i\widetilde{r}_{i} and destination zjz_{j} by

λt(i,j)=1t𝟏{i=j}.\lambda_{t}(i,j)=\frac{1}{t}\mathbf{1}\{i=j\}. (6.4)

Every row and column sums to 1/t1/t, so this is a feasible plan from D^t\widehat{D}_{t} to ν^t\widehat{\nu}_{t}. Its cost is t−1​∑i=1td⁡(r~i,zi)t^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{t}d(\widetilde{r}_{i},z_{i}), so

W1​(D^t,ν^t)≤1t​∑i=1td⁡(r~i,zi).W_{1}(\widehat{D}_{t},\widehat{\nu}_{t})\leq\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}d(\widetilde{r}_{i},z_{i}). (6.5)

Adding transport from ν^t\widehat{\nu}_{t} to ν\nu and taking expectations gives

𝔼⁡[W1​(D^t,ν)]≤W1​(D,ν)+ft,\mathbb{E}[W_{1}(\widehat{D}_{t},\nu)]\leq W_{1}(D,\nu)+f_{t},

proving (6.2).

Finally, let σ\sigma be an optimal matching of (r~1,…,r~n)(\widetilde{r}_{1},\ldots,\widetilde{r}_{n}) to SS. Match each ziz_{i} to sσ⁡(i)s_{\sigma(i)} as well. This is feasible, because the server labels σ⁡(i)\sigma(i) are all distinct. Therefore,

OPT⁡((z1,…,zn),S)\displaystyle\mathrm{OPT}((z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}),S) ≤∑i=1nd⁡(zi,sσ⁡(i))≤∑i=1nd⁡(zi,r~i)+OPT⁡((r~1,…,r~n),S).\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}d(z_{i},s_{\sigma(i)})\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}d(z_{i},\widetilde{r}_{i})+\mathrm{OPT}((\widetilde{r}_{1},\ldots,\widetilde{r}_{n}),S).

Taking expectations and using (6.1) proves (6.3). ∎

We now combine these inequalities with Theorem 4.3 to obtain the competitive-ratio bound.

Theorem 6.2.

Suppose Fair-Bias is α⁡(n)\alpha(n)-competitive for requests drawn independently from ν\nu on the server placements under consideration. Then Algorithm 1 satisfies

𝔼⁡[ALG]≤(1+6​α​(n))​𝔼​[OPT]\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{ALG}]\leq(1+6\alpha(n))\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{OPT}] (6.6)

for every unknown i.i.d. request distribution on a finite metric space.

Proof.

By (5.6), (6.2), and Theorem 4.3,

𝔼⁡[ALG]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{ALG}] ≤∑t=1n𝔼⁡[W1​(D^t,ν)]+∑k=1ngk≤n​W1​(D,ν)+∑t=1nft+∑k=1ngk\displaystyle\leq\sum_{t=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}[W_{1}(\widehat{D}_{t},\nu)]+\sum_{k=1}^{n}g_{k}\leq nW_{1}(D,\nu)+\sum_{t=1}^{n}f_{t}+\sum_{k=1}^{n}g_{k}
≤n​W1​(D,ν)+3​∑k=1ngk≤n​W1​(D,ν)+3​α​(n)​𝔼​[OPTν]\displaystyle\leq nW_{1}(D,\nu)+3\sum_{k=1}^{n}g_{k}\leq nW_{1}(D,\nu)+3\alpha(n)\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{OPT}_{\nu}]
≤𝔼⁡[OPT]+6​α​(n)​𝔼​[OPT].\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{OPT}]+6\alpha(n)\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{OPT}].

The last line uses (6.1) and (6.3). ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Combining Theorems 6.2 and 3.2 gives the stated asymptotic ratio on finite metric spaces. The reduction in Section 2.1 gives the same asymptotic ratio on arbitrary metric spaces. ∎

For tree metrics, substituting α⁡(n)=4\alpha(n)=4 from Proposition 3.2 into Theorem 6.2 gives a constant competitive ratio.

Corollary 6.3.

On tree metrics, unknown i.i.d. requests can be served with competitive ratio 5151, with no restriction on the support of the request distribution. If the request distribution has finite support, Algorithm 1 is 2525-competitive.

Proof.

If DD has finite support, its support together with the server locations forms a finite metric space, so Theorem 6.2 gives 1+6⋅4=251+6\cdot 4=25. The reduction in Section 2.1 gives 2⋅25+1=512\cdot 25+1=51 for arbitrary request distributions. ∎

7 Comparison with random-order arrivals

As summarized in Table 1, the upper bounds in Theorems 1.1 and 6.3 are asymptotically smaller than the random-order lower bound [11].

Lemma 5.1 holds for a uniformly random ordering of any fixed multiset. It is therefore important to identify why the competitive analysis cannot simply be repeated for random-order inputs. The obstruction is the comparison in (6.3) between the offline optimum for nn independent requests from ν\nu and the offline optimum for the actual requests: exchangeability alone does not imply that comparison.

For example, take two servers at 00 and 11 with distance one, and let the random-order request multiset be M={0,1}M=\{0,1\}. Its empirical distribution is DM=νD_{M}=\nu, and

OPT⁡(M,S)=0,W1​(DM,ν)=0.\mathrm{OPT}(M,S)=0,\qquad W_{1}(D_{M},\nu)=0.

However, two independent requests from ν\nu coincide with probability 1/21/2; when they do, their optimal matching cost is one. Hence

𝔼⁡[OPTν]=12>OPT⁡(M,S)+n​W1​(DM,ν)=0.\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{OPT}_{\nu}]=\frac{1}{2}>\mathrm{OPT}(M,S)+nW_{1}(D_{M},\nu)=0.

Thus the counterpart of (6.3) is false in the random-order model. The exact generation of independent virtual inputs by itself is not a competitive-ratio guarantee; the conversion cost must also be charged to an appropriate offline benchmark.

Appendix A Leaving common mass in place

We use the matrix representation of transport plans from Section 2.2.

Lemma A.1.

Let (pi)(p_{i}) and (qi)(q_{i}) be nonnegative masses of the same total mass on a finite label set. With transport cost d⁡(si,sj)d(s_{i},s_{j}), an optimal plan may be chosen so that

γ⁡(i,i)=min⁡{pi,qi}for every ​i.\gamma(i,i)=\min\{p_{i},q_{i}\}\quad\text{for every }i.
Proof.

The feasible set of transport plans is nonempty and compact. Among its cost-minimizing plans, choose one maximizing the total diagonal mass ∑iγ⁡(i,i)\sum_{i}\gamma(i,i). If at some label vv, γ⁡(v,v)<min⁡{pv,qv}\gamma(v,v)<\min\{p_{v},q_{v}\}, then there exist u≠vu\neq v and w≠vw\neq v with γ⁡(u,v)>0\gamma(u,v)>0 and γ⁡(v,w)>0\gamma(v,w)>0. Let

ε=min⁡{γ⁡(u,v),γ⁡(v,w)}>0.\varepsilon=\min\{\gamma(u,v),\gamma(v,w)\}>0.

Decrease γ⁡(u,v)\gamma(u,v) and γ⁡(v,w)\gamma(v,w) by ε\varepsilon, and increase γ⁡(u,w)\gamma(u,w) and γ⁡(v,v)\gamma(v,v) by ε\varepsilon. The source row sums and destination column sums are unchanged, and no entry becomes negative. The cost change is

ε⁡(d⁡(su,sw)−d⁡(su,sv)−d⁡(sv,sw))≤0.\varepsilon\bigl(d(s_{u},s_{w})-d(s_{u},s_{v})-d(s_{v},s_{w})\bigr)\leq 0.

Thus the modified plan is still optimal. Its diagonal mass has increased by ε\varepsilon, or by 2​ε2\varepsilon if u=wu=w, contradicting the choice of γ\gamma. Hence all diagonal entries equal the common mass. ∎

After that common mass is removed, only labels with excess source mass need send mass, and only labels with excess destination mass need receive it. This is the residual transport used in Lemma 4.1.
